h: A small city with a big sense of history
p: Armagh punches well above its size. It's the ecclesiastical capital of Ireland, linked to St Patrick, and it has not one but two St Patrick's cathedrals, one Church of Ireland and one Catholic, each on its own hill facing the other across the city. Both are striking buildings, and seeing them is a natural add-on to a morning under the planetarium dome.

Down on the Mall, a long, leafy green fringed with Georgian terraces, you'll find Armagh County Museum, which digs into the history and people of the county. Bookish visitors should also seek out the Armagh Robinson Library, founded in 1771 by Archbishop Richard Robinson, the same churchman behind the observatory. It's a lovely link between the two sites and a reminder of how much the city owes to one ambitious founder.

Just outside the city, Navan Fort is an ancient earthwork tied up with the legends of Ulster's old kings. There's not a great deal of structure to see, but the setting and the stories are rich, and it makes a good leg-stretch in fresh air.

Visiting in spring? Armagh is known as the Orchard County, and the blossom on the apple trees around the countryside is a lovely sight. Keep an eye out for local Bramley apple products in shops and cafés, which make a tasty souvenir.
Planning-wise, give the observatory site a good half day if you want a show, the exhibitions and a proper potter round the Astropark, and leave the afternoon for the city.
